title: What Success Means
author: Is It Working?!
summary: Drawing on a 30-country, 22,693-respondent Ipsos survey published in summer 2026, this piece dismantles the widely-repeated narrative that young people have disengaged from work and reoriented around meaning over stability, showing instead that Gen Z, Millennials, Gen X, and Baby Boomers all rank a stable full-time job as the top marker of success at nearly identical rates (61-67%), well ahead of marriage or parenthood. The real generational difference isn't values but confidence: each successive generation is less certain it will actually reach the milestones it wants, which Ipsos frames precisely as a question of attainability rather than abandoned aspiration. The piece then marshals a substantial body of occupational-psychology evidence to argue that organizations vastly underweight the emotional stakes of job insecurity -- unemployment carries roughly double the rate of psychological problems as employment, a 15-year longitudinal study of over 24,000 Germans found life satisfaction never fully recovers even after re-employment, and financial scarcity itself measurably consumes cognitive capacity (an effect equivalent to about 13 IQ points in one study of Indian farmers before versus after harvest income). Its concluding, practically-oriented section argues that corporate wellbeing programs misfire because they treat identical resilience interventions as relevant to executives with savings cushions and hourly workers with none, when the Ipsos income breakdown shows security is sharply unevenly distributed (a 30-point gap in already-having a stable job between high- and low-income households) and recommends employers instead measure and communicate around insecurity directly rather than assuming it away.
points: The generational data directly refutes the 'young people have disengaged from work' narrative: Gen Z (66%), Millennials (67%), Gen X (65%), and Boomers (61%) rank a stable job as the top success marker at nearly identical rates -- the real difference is confidence in attaining it, not the underlying value.

The Lucas et al. 15-year, 24,000-person German longitudinal study is the piece's most consequential finding: life satisfaction after unemployment recovers only partially and never returns to its prior baseline, even once a person is re-employed, meaning the psychological scar of job loss outlasts the job loss itself.

Mani et al.'s Science study on Indian sugarcane farmers (worse cognitive performance pre-harvest when poor versus post-harvest when paid, an effect equivalent to roughly 13 IQ points) is used to argue financial insecurity is not just stressful but directly degrades the cognitive capacity an employee needs to do their job well -- creating a self-fulfilling spiral when employers respond to insecurity with more insecurity.

The practical recommendation to 'segment your wellbeing spend by exposure, not by grade' directly targets a specific corporate failure mode: identical resilience-app interventions offered equally to an executive with savings and an hourly worker without one are not equally relevant, since the Ipsos data shows security itself is sharply unequally distributed by income (a 30-point job-attainment gap between high- and low-income households).
quotes: The answer, at the top of the list, on 65%: having a stable, full-time job. Not marriage (25%), becoming a parent (31%) or even owning your own home (58%).
In Western markets, 66% of Gen Z name a stable full-time job as a marker of success. Millennials: 67%. Gen X: 65%. Baby Boomers: 61%. There is NO values gap.
Ipsos put the conclusion in a single beautiful sentence: these are not questions of abandoning traditional values, they're questions of attainability.

Lucas, Clark, Georgellis and Diener tracked more than 24,000 Germans over fifteen years and found that people hit by unemployment dropped sharply in life satisfaction, recovered partially, and never fully returned to their previous level, even after they were re-employed.

The same Indian sugarcane farmers performed measurably worse on reasoning and cognitive-control tasks before harvest, when poor, than after it, when paid -- an effect the authors put at roughly the equivalent of 13 IQ points.

Higher-income households are more likely to say a stable full-time job matters (70% versus 60% of low-income households), much more likely to have already got one (82% versus 52%; a shocking 30pt gap).
